title: Quashing of FIR - when High Courts actually intervene
p1:
Can an FIR be cancelled even before the trial begins?

Many people believe once an FIR is registered, the accused has no option left. But that is not always true.
p2:
The High Court has the power to quash an FIR in certain situations, but it does not act like an appeal court deciding who is guilty or innocent. Its role is to prevent misuse of the legal process.

A surprising fact: even a genuine-looking FIR can be stopped if the allegations, on their face, do not disclose any offence or if continuing the case would amount to harassment.
p3:
For example, if a complaint is filed only to settle a personal dispute or the facts mentioned do not legally constitute a crime, the High Court may intervene under its inherent powers.

But quashing is not automatic. Courts carefully examine the facts and step in only when there is a clear reason to prevent injustice.
conclusion: Do you think High Courts should have wider powers to stop false FIRs at an early stage?
